newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian interest rates need to be brought down - RBI.
newsitem.headline: Indian interest rates need to be brought down - RBI.

text.p: Interest rates need to be brought down to a level consistent with the rate of inflation if investments are to be sustained, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Deputy Governor S.S.Tarapore said on Friday.
"The present high real rates of interest are a major concern as at these high real interest rates, investments cannot be viable," Tarapore told a meeting of businessmen.
An interest rate structure which was appropriate when inflation rates were in double digits was obviously not appropriate when inflation rates had been reduced by more than half, he said.
The rate of inflation has come down from double-digit levels last year to around five percent this year.
Tarapore said the demand for funds was high with the economy straining at the leash and as financial intermediaries competed for funds, there was a tendency to raise the price of money.
But in a progressively deregulated environment, financial intermediaries would have to be sensitive to signals from the market, he cautioned.
It had become evident in recent times that borrowers were cutting down on their credit demands from banks and financial institutions, he said.
"There could well be a direct tapping of the market by corporates, especially for short-term funds."

"It would be in the best interests of financial intermediaries to reduce the interest rate structure on both their liabilities as well as assets and this would enable the interest rate structure to move to a level consistent with the lower inflation rate," Tarapore said.
While there were arguments in favour of the RBI allowing a larger primary money creation, this would not solve the problem of high interest rates, he said.
"Far from resolving the problem of high real interest rates, it would merely fuel inflation rates and thereby force up nominal rates of interest," Tarapore said.
To ensure that interest rates were at reasonable levels, it was essential that monetary-fiscal policies were committed to inflation control, he said.
"Corporates, in turn, must learn to economise on credit by improved cash management and this would also assist in bringing down interest rates."
Developments in financial 1996/97 (April-March) were encouraging with indications that the liquidity crunch which hit industry in 1995/96 had eased, he said.
